title: Evaluating Misinformation on YouTube about Washing Produce Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of 100 YouTube produce-washing videos coded factual vs nonfactual against an external ground truth (CDC and Health Canada safe food handling recommendations: wash produce only under running water; no room-temperature storage of pre-cut/ready-to-eat produce beyond 2 h). 70 of 100 videos contained nonfactual information - a share of items judged inaccurate against stated guidelines, with a clear denominator, i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate. This is guideline-concordance coding explicitly framed as factual/nonfactual, so it is CONTENT rather than QUALITY under §3.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language (or English-subtitled) YouTube videos, coded against U.S. CDC and Health Canada recommendations, authors based in Canada. Limitation: "only English videos were analyzed; this potential language bias limits our findings to English-speaking countries"
estimates.date: Videos retrieved October 2021; upload dates 6 June 2008-9 April 2019 (prepandemic, n=34) and 17 March 2020-23 September 2021 (pandemic, n=66)
estimates.measure_type: % of produce-washing YouTube videos containing nonfactual information about washing produce or storing it at room temperature
estimates.value_raw: Of the 100 videos, 70 contained nonfactual information (70/100 = 70%); Table 3 confirms Nonfactual (N = 70) vs Factual (N = 30)
estimates.denominator: 100 YouTube videos on washing fruits and/or vegetables in a household setting, in English or with English subtitles and with more than 1,000 views, retrieved with three targeted search terms and sorted by view count (66 posted during the pandemic, 34 before)
estimates.definition: Video coded nonfactual if the washing or storage practice it used or recommended departed from CDC / Health Canada guidance - i.e. it recommended washing produce with soap (incl. vegetable washes), vinegar, salt, baking soda, spices, lemon/lime, or 'other' agents (potassium permanganate, isopropyl alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, toothpaste, essential oils, dishwasher) rather than running water alone, or recommended storing pre-cut/ready-to-eat produce at room temperature for more than 2 h
estimates.misinfo_def: "Videos were classified as 'factual' if they corresponded to safe food handling recommendations from the CDC and Health Canada, including washing produce only with running water and not storing pre-cut or ready-to-eat produce at room temperature for >2 h (6, 16)."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 100 videos, 70 contained nonfactual information regarding food safety techniques for washing fruits and vegetables or storing produce at room temperature.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Descriptive results', p. 163 (denominators corroborated by Table 3: Nonfactual N = 70, Factual N = 30; also Abstract)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: One researcher independently coded produce-washing practices in all 100 videos against published CDC and Health Canada produce-safety recommendations, and a second researcher validated the coding ('After one researcher independently coded produce washing practices on all the videos, a second researcher validated the coding'); no inter-rater reliability statistic is reported, and the Acknowledgment thanks a further person for assistance with coding validation.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data collection took place by searching for relevant videos on YouTube in October 2021. The targeted search terms used were "how to wash fruits and vegetables," "fruits and vegetables washing techniques," and "food washing techniques during the COVID-19 pandemic." For each search term used, the videos were sorted by view count. The inclusion criteria were that the videos must be in English or have English subtitles, have more than 1,000 views, and cover washing of produce (fruits and/or vegetables) in a household setting.
estimates.notes: Pooled across both upload periods, which is the paper's only whole-corpus figure. The pandemic subsample is markedly higher: 'Among videos posted during the COVID-19 pandemic, 55 (83%) contained nonfactual information' (55/66). The prepandemic nonfactual share is never stated; Table 1 gives only 'Factual 19 (55.9)' for the 34 prepandemic videos, and 100 - 55.9 would be a computed complement, forbidden by R8. The abstract's 'Videos posted during the pandemic were more likely to have nonfactual information than those posted before the pandemic (56 versus 17%)' cannot be reconciled with Table 1 or with the 83% in the Results and looks like a transposition of the FACTUAL row (16.7% vs 55.9%); the 70/100 used here is unaffected. denom_selection=curated because videos were rank-truncated (sorted by view count) and filtered to >1,000 views, which biases the sample toward popular videos. topic coded health_other (food-safety practice) rather than covid19: a third of the corpus predates the pandemic and the veracity standard is generic produce-safety guidance, though covid19 would be defensible for the during-pandemic subsample, whose framing is COVID transmission via produce.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the during-pandemic subsample share, 55 (83%) of 66 videos - a time-window subgroup of the row above; recorded in the row's notes rather than as its own row per the collapse-the-time-series rule. (2) The prepandemic nonfactual share - not stated, and only derivable as a complement of Table 1's 'Factual 19 (55.9)', which R8 forbids. (3) Table 4's source subgroups, 'YouTube videos posted by individual bloggers were more likely to contain nonfactual information than videos posted by government agencies and other organizations (78.3 versus 29.4%)' - uploader-type subgroups, not the paper's whole-corpus prevalence, and their denominators (83 blogger videos, 17 government/organisation videos) are sample composition. (4) The technique shares among the 66 pandemic videos (vinegar 45.5%, salt 33.3%, baking soda 28.8%, soap 25.8%, 'other' 24.2%, lemon 7.6%, temperature abuse 7.6%, spices 6.1%) - overlapping component practices inside the same videos (median 2 incorrect techniques per pandemic video), so they are sub-definitions of the nonfactual coding, not separate estimates, and they cannot be summed. (5) Sample composition (83% bloggers, 12% organisations, 5% government) and the engagement medians in Tables 2-3 - not veracity shares. (6) Figures cited from other studies, excluded by R8: 'an estimated 23 to 26% of health-related YouTube videos contained nonfactual information about the COVID-19 virus' (ref 9), '19% of participants reported washing foods with bleach' (ref 5), 'over 70% of adults rely on the Internet for health information' (ref 9). Uncertainty for the adjudicator: country coding. No country is stated anywhere; I coded Global/global because the sampling frame is English-language YouTube worldwide, but the ground truth is U.S./Canadian guidance and the authors limit generalisability to 'English-speaking countries', so a Multi-country coding is arguable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis, searched October 2021 with three targeted phrases, results sorted by view count; inclusion required English or English subtitles, >1,000 views and household produce washing; 100 videos analysed (66 pandemic uploads, median 22 April 2020; 34 prepandemic, median 19 February 2015). Coding: washing agents and temperature abuse recorded per video and judged against CDC and Health Canada recommendations; ONE researcher coded all videos and a SECOND validated the coding, with no kappa or percent-agreement reported. Analysis in R (chi-square/Fisher for categorical, Wilcoxon rank-sum for skewed continuous measures). Acknowledged limitations: English-only, only three search terms ('some additional popular videos could have been missed'), single primary coder; the two upload periods span very different windows (11 years vs 18 months), which the authors note confounds the view-count comparison; no sampling frame beyond relevance/view-count ranking, so the 100 videos are not a random sample of produce-washing videos.
rob.item6_quote: Videos were classified as "factual" if they corresponded to safe food handling recommendations from the CDC and Health Canada, including washing produce only with running water and not storing pre-cut or ready-to-eat produce at room temperature for >2 h (6, 16).
rob.item10_quote: Of the 100 videos, 70 contained nonfactual information regarding food safety techniques for washing fruits and vegetables or storing produce at room temperature.
